periods.title: The Deccan before Swarajya
periods.summary: The Adil Shahi and Nizam Shahi courts and the Mughal advance shaped opportunities for landed families, military service and negotiations.

periods.title: The formation of Swarajya
periods.summary: Fort acquisition, diplomacy and the assertion of royal authority gave Shivaji Maharaj a base against competing powers.

periods.title: Succession and resistance
periods.summary: Sambhaji, Rajaram and Tarabai faced an expanding Mughal military presence. Leadership moved when a capital or fort could no longer serve.

periods.title: Rival courts and revenue rights
periods.summary: Shahu’s release opened a fight over succession. His court made agreements about tribute and revenue while the Kolhapur line retained authority.

periods.title: Expansion and administration
periods.summary: Maratha chiefs and revenue agents operated across different regions. Peshwa authority interacted with local elites and other ruling houses.

periods.title: The north, Panipat and the return
periods.summary: The campaign depended on other rulers, supply, money and movement. Defeat interrupted the northern push, which was later renewed.

periods.title: Regional powers and Company rivalry
periods.summary: Shinde, Holkar, Gaikwad and Bhonsle interests diverged. The Peshwa and the East India Company became entangled in competing agreements.

periods.title: Company treaties and war
periods.summary: Successive agreements increased Company leverage. War in 1817–18 ended the Peshwa’s political authority.

periods.title: Authority continues in other forms
periods.summary: Satara retained a ruling house under Company paramountcy until annexation. The end of the Peshwa’s government did not end Maratha political and social institutions.

places.name: Deccan sultanate country
places.summary: No fixed frontier drawn. Offices, forts and estates had different holders at different dates.

places.name: Pratapgad
places.summary: A hill-forest fort in the UNESCO property. The marker orients the reader to the site.

places.name: Agra
places.summary: The point does not identify the building in which Shivaji was detained.

places.name: Raigad
places.summary: A capital site with fortified approaches, palace and market areas and provision for water.

places.name: Rajgad
places.summary: A separate hill-fort component near Raigad. The point shows geography and terrain context.

places.name: Suvarnadurg
places.summary: A fortified coastal position in the same modern heritage collection.

places.name: Gingee
places.summary: The Tamil Nadu component of the inscribed property. Used here to orient the reader to Rajaram’s southern base.

places.name: Satara
places.summary: Orientation point for Shahu’s court and the later princely state.

places.name: Vasai (Bassein)
places.summary: The names Vasai and Bassein refer to the same place in different records. It has distinct episodes of military seizure, revenue and diplomacy.

places.name: Pune
places.summary: Orientation point for the Peshwa’s government and the 1817 treaty.

places.name: Delhi
places.summary: The point orients the northern campaign and the 1719 documentary context. It does not trace the route of the armies.

places.name: Panipat
places.summary: The city is a reference for the campaign and battle. Camp extent and precise movements are unresolved in this map.

places.name: Kunjpura
places.summary: The district gazetteer names the locality in the October 1760 campaign. No battle footprint is drawn.

places.name: Khed in the succession account
places.summary: The gazetteer names Khed. No exact battlefield position is assigned here.

events.title: Service and power in the Deccan
events.summary: The royal houses of Bijapur and Ahmadnagar, Mughal officers and local military families negotiated overlapping rights and service. Shahaji’s career belongs to this context.
events.consequence: How service, landholding and family networks created room for a new polity.

events.title: Confrontation at Pratapgad
events.summary: Bijapur sent Afzal Khan against Shivaji. Their confrontation at Pratapgad became a turning point in the contest over forts and authority.
events.consequence: The site is a named fort. Accounts of the encounter and its details require their own witnesses.

events.title: Agra and the escape
events.authority: Mughal custody and a Maratha ruler
events.summary: Letters from Jaipur’s representatives record Shivaji’s escape. Accounts give different amounts of detail on how it occurred.
events.consequence: The evidence trail separates knowledge of the escape, the basket story and the missing itinerary.

events.title: Coronation at Raigad
events.summary: The coronation made Raigad a ceremonial and administrative centre. The hilltop also needed a way to receive people, store water and sustain a working market.
events.consequence: The Raigad lesson connects those needs to modern terrain and documented structures.

events.title: Sambhaji and Mughal pressure
events.summary: Sambhaji succeeded Shivaji and faced Aurangzeb’s southward campaigns. His capture and execution in 1689 brought another crisis for the court.
events.consequence: Authority had to endure when a ruler and a capital could be lost. Raigad is a court reference for this period.

events.title: Rajaram’s southern base
events.summary: Rajaram reached the fortified base at Gingee under Mughal pressure in the Deccan. The southern stronghold let leadership continue while operations elsewhere remained contested.
events.consequence: The change of base is supported. The explorer leaves the intermediate escape route open.

events.title: Tarabai organizes resistance
events.authority: Tarabai and the claim of her son
events.summary: After Rajaram’s death, Tarabai acted for her young son and maintained a competing claim to rule during the struggle with the Mughals.
events.consequence: Her decisions and the loyalties of military commanders remained consequential after Aurangzeb died.

events.title: Allegiance changes at Khed
events.authority: Rival claims of Shahu and Tarabai
events.summary: As Shahu advanced, Dhanaji Jadhav did not engage his force, according to the district gazetteer. Parashurampant Pratinidhi withdrew toward Satara.
events.consequence: The change in allegiance advanced Shahu’s claim and connects the campaign to his later installation at Satara.

events.title: Shahu returns and claims the throne
events.summary: Released after Aurangzeb’s death, Sambhaji’s son Shahu claimed the throne. Some commanders supported him, while Tarabai held to the claim of her own son.
events.consequence: Satara and Kolhapur developed distinct courts. A claimant’s allies and a fort’s garrison can tell different stories.

events.title: A right to collect revenue
events.summary: Grants secured through Balaji Vishwanath’s mission recognized claims to chauth and sardeshmukhi from six Deccan provinces. These were revenue claims that had to be collected in practice.
events.consequence: The document’s claim does not give a boundary for daily control or say who paid each assessment.

events.title: Vasai changes hands
events.authority: Chimaji Appa’s force and Portuguese Bassein
events.summary: After a siege led by Chimaji Appa, the Portuguese lost Vasai. The change concerned a fort and a port with commercial and administrative needs.
events.consequence: A surviving port account from the same year opens a different question from who won the siege.

events.title: A port ledger records trade and diplomacy
events.authority: Shankaraji Keshav, port administration under the Peshwas
events.summary: The account records money and goods credited after the seizure of English ships in the previous year. It then records an instruction to return the goods because relations were friendly.
events.consequence: The ledger shows how an order about diplomatic relations affected what the port could keep. It dates a fiscal record after the change of control.

events.title: Shahu chooses Balaji Baji Rao
events.summary: After Baji Rao died, Shahu appointed his son Balaji Baji Rao. The Peshwa’s office became increasingly influential as operations extended into northern and eastern regions.
events.consequence: Different regions were administered through chiefs, allied elites and revenue agents. Influence varied by place and arrangement.

events.title: The move from Delhi to Kunjpura
events.summary: Bhāu’s force moved from Delhi towards Kunjpura. Blocking sources of money and provisions was a concern for both sides along the Yamunā.
events.consequence: A success at Kunjpura did not settle the river crossings and the routes supplies would have to take afterward.

events.title: The camp loses supply access
events.summary: Interdiction made food and fodder harder to bring into the Maratha camp. The burden extended to non-combatant followers and to animals needed for transport.
events.consequence: The district account supports the direction of the change. Exact population and loss estimates are disputed.

events.title: The Third Battle of Panipat
events.summary: Ahmad Shah Durrani’s coalition defeated the Maratha expedition. The Rohilla leaders and Shujāʿ al-Dawla had their own political interests in joining the coalition.
events.consequence: The defeat brought losses far beyond the battlefield and interrupted the northern expedition.

events.title: A renewed northern campaign
events.summary: Later Maratha intervention in the north restored influence around Delhi. It depended on leadership, funding and new negotiations.
events.consequence: The political consequences of Panipat involved years of recovery and shifting agreements.

events.title: Regional houses take different paths
events.summary: Military leaders and family houses built power bases with different ties to the Peshwa’s court. They negotiated with local rulers and increasingly with the Company.
events.consequence: The atlas leaves territorial boundaries open. A treaty or tribute relation can coexist with another authority in the same area.

events.title: Treaty of Bassein
events.authority: Baji Rao II and the East India Company
events.summary: Baji Rao II sought Company support after defeat near Pune. The treaty provided for a subsidiary force and limited independent dealings with European rivals.
events.consequence: Other Maratha houses made their own choices about an agreement that constrained the Peshwa.

events.title: The Poona Treaty narrows the Peshwa’s options
events.authority: Baji Rao II and Company Resident Elphinstone
events.summary: The archive lists a contemporary comparison of the Poona Treaty with Bassein. The agreement came before renewed fighting in 1817–18.
events.consequence: The paired documents let a reader distinguish formal restrictions from the subsequent outcome of the war.

events.title: The Peshwa’s government ends
events.authority: Company rule after the third war
events.summary: The Company defeated and displaced Baji Rao II. The change ended the Peshwa’s government and rearranged relations with other authorities.
events.consequence: Satara continued under a different arrangement, so the political change has more than one endpoint.

events.title: Satara under Company paramountcy
events.authority: Satara ruling house and Company authority
events.summary: Satara’s ruling house held a princely state under Company paramountcy after the Peshwa’s government ended. Annexation followed in 1848.
events.consequence: The political period ends in 1818 in the main track. Satara’s history shows which institutions continued and under what terms.

dossiers.title: How much could the fort supply itself?
dossiers.summary: The ICOMOS evaluation identifies water harvesting and features used by a working capital. A high protected platform still needs reliable water storage, food deliveries and market space. Compare these needs with the seven modern elevation samples.

dossiers.title: Hill forts in the network
dossiers.summary: Compare the site types for Raigad and Rajgad with the very different terrain of a fort guarding a coastal approach. This geographic comparison does not assert a dated supply road between them.

dossiers.title: What can a fortified coastal site protect?
dossiers.summary: Suvarnadurg is a maritime component of the UNESCO property. Its position shaped access by sea. For the accounting side of coastal control, compare the separate Vasai port record.

dossiers.title: What changes when a port changes hands?
dossiers.summary: Appendix C-2 reproduces an account for the Bassein port under Shankaraji Keshav in 1739. A siege changes possession. Accounts illuminate the administrative task that follows, including how receipts and expenditures are recorded.
